Carpets In Parallelogram

GeometryAreaConstructions
Game: This is a picture, not a game: the coloured parts change when you drag the points, but the difference between the red and the blue never changes.
How to play: Drag the corners A, B, C and D or the points P, Q and R, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Tick “Hint” to see the pink and orange pieces, and “Names” to label the points.
Look for the math

Drag any point and the coloured pieces change shape: some grow, some shrink. Yet when you take the blue piece away from all the red pieces, the number left over is always half the parallelogram. Here is why.

Two big triangles

Forget P and R for a moment. Point Q sits on the top side CD. The triangle ADQ has the same base as the whole box and reaches from top to bottom, so it covers exactly half. The triangle BCQ does the same. Together they cover half the parallelogram:

RED = Area(ADQ) + Area(BCQ) = Area(ABCD) / 2

This is the page's first claim, and the logic test checks it for thousands of shapes.

The carpet pieces

The cutting lines divide those two big triangles into four red pieces, with a pink triangle cut out of each. In between them sits the blue pentagon STUVW, and below them the orange triangle ABW. Tick “Hint” to see the two pink triangles and the orange one. The trapezoid ABPR is a carpet: its diagonals swap equal areas. The page calls this equation (1):

Area(RST) + BLUE + Area(PUV) = Area(ABW)

So the pink pieces together with the blue pentagon make exactly the orange triangle. The logic test checks this equality on every drawn picture in its sample.

Why the difference is constant

The four red pieces plus the orange triangle are what is left of the two big triangles after the pink pieces are removed. Taking away the blue pentagon gives

RED − Area(RST) − Area(PUV) + Area(ABW) − BLUE = RED

because of (1). And RED is half the parallelogram. That is the exact claim on the page: painted red minus blue = Area(ABCD) / 2, whatever the positions of P, Q and R. The test also moves P, Q and R through 500 fresh positions on one parallelogram and gets the same number every time.

Small details

When two cutting lines run parallel, the applet's intersection routine returns “not a number” and the Java version hides the carpet. This page does the same; the status line says so. One deliberate change: the applet let P, Q and R slide along the whole side line and hid the drawing when a point left its side, while here they stay on the side segments, so the carpet remains as the page describes it. The checkboxes also start unchecked, as in the applet: tick “Hint” to see the pink and orange pieces used in the proof.

Try this: tick “Names”, drag Q towards D, then drag the bottom-left corner sideways. The coloured pieces rearrange, but the two numbers in the status line still match.
